name: Digital Logic
description: Number systems, Boolean algebra, minimisation, combinational and sequential circuits, lesson by lesson from the GATE notes.

zones.name: Number systems, codes and floating point

nodes.name: Place value & bases
nodes.desc: Place value and changing bases. Positional value and the digit limit; base → decimal (expansion, Horner); decimal → base (repeated division, uniqueness proof); base → base
nodes.summary: You will be able to convert numbers between any two bases and solve problems where the base itself is the unknown.
topics: Repeated division to write base b
Converting from one base to another
Digits needed to represent a number

nodes.name: Binary, octal & hex
nodes.desc: Binary, octal and hex: grouping and arithmetic. The grouping theorem (k-bit groups from the point); octal ↔ hex via binary; base 4; powers-of-16 sums read as hex; popcount per hex digit
nodes.summary: You will be able to convert between binary, octal, hex and base 4 by grouping bits and do arithmetic directly in these bases.
topics: Octal, hex and base 4 via binary

nodes.name: Fractions & fixed point
nodes.desc: Fractions and fixed-point numbers. Fraction → base b by repeated multiplication; mixed numbers; the terminating vs recurring theorem; truncation error
nodes.summary: You will be able to convert fractions into any base, decide which fractions terminate, and represent values in fixed point with known truncation error.
topics: Converting a fraction into base b

nodes.name: Signed numbers
nodes.desc: Signed numbers and complements. Unsigned; sign-magnitude; 1's complement; 2's complement (−2^{n−1} weight, invert + 1, copy-to-first-1); ranges and counts; two zeros; decoding
nodes.summary: You will be able to read n-bit patterns as unsigned, sign-magnitude, 1's complement, 2's complement or biased values and spot overflow.
topics: Four ways to read n bits

nodes.name: Floating point basics
nodes.desc: Floating point: normalisation, biased exponents and range. Scientific notation in base 2 and 16; mantissa/significand, exponent and bias (excess-K); normalisation and the hidden bit
nodes.summary: You will be able to encode and decode a custom floating-point format using normalisation and a biased exponent, and work out its range and precision.
topics: Encoding and decoding a custom format
Range, precision and gaps between neighbours

nodes.name: IEEE-754
nodes.desc: IEEE-754 single and double precision. The single and double layouts; bias 127/1023; encode and decode; special values (±0, ±∞, NaN); denormals; largest and smallest values; reading hex words quickly
nodes.summary: You will be able to encode and decode IEEE-754 single and double precision values, including special values, denormals and the extreme representable numbers.

nodes.name: Float arithmetic
nodes.desc: Floating-point arithmetic, rounding and overflow. Add/subtract (align, add, normalise, round); multiply/divide (add/subtract exponents); multiplying by powers of two; rounding and absorption; non-associativity
nodes.summary: You will be able to carry out floating-point addition, subtraction, multiplication and division with rounding and recognise absorption, cancellation and overflow.

nodes.name: Binary codes
nodes.desc: Binary codes: BCD, excess-3, Gray, parity and Hamming. Weighted vs unweighted codes (8421, 2421, 84−2−1); BCD validity; self-complementing codes; excess-3; reflected Gray (construction, conversions, unit distance)
nodes.summary: You will be able to use BCD and other decimal codes, self-complementing codes and Gray code, and apply parity and Hamming codes to detect and correct errors.

nodes.name: Code arithmetic
nodes.desc: Arithmetic with number codes. Binary add/subtract (borrows), shift-and-add multiplication, long division; add/subtract/ multiply in base 8, 16 and any base b
nodes.summary: You will be able to perform binary and base-b arithmetic, subtract with complements and add in BCD and excess-3 with the right corrections.
topics: Binary addition, subtraction, multiplication and division

nodes.name: Booth's algorithm
nodes.desc: Signed multiplication and Booth's algorithm. Shift-and-add for unsigned and signed operands (sign-extended partial products; the multiplier's sign bit weighs −2ⁿ⁻¹); product bits as Boolean functions
nodes.summary: You will be able to multiply signed numbers by shift-and-add and by Booth recoding, and count the additions and subtractions Booth's algorithm needs.

nodes.name: Logic gates
nodes.desc: Logic gates and truth tables. NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR (symbols, truth tables, multi-input forms); bubbles and active-low; positive vs negative logic; buffers
nodes.summary: You will be able to read and evaluate circuits built from the basic and derived logic gates, including active-low signals and negative logic.
topics: Bubbles, active-low signals and De Morgan
Reading a circuit gate by gate

nodes.name: Boolean laws
nodes.desc: Boolean algebra: postulates, laws and theorems. Huntington postulates; identity, complement, idempotence, involution, absorption, distributivity (both forms), De Morgan, consensus, duality
nodes.summary: You will be able to simplify, prove and disprove Boolean identities using the postulates, De Morgan's laws, consensus and Shannon expansion.

nodes.name: XOR algebra
nodes.desc: XOR/XNOR algebra and custom operators. XOR/XNOR laws (a ⊕ a = 0, a ⊕ 1 = ā, associativity, complementing inputs); parity functions; XNOR as equivalence
nodes.summary: You will be able to manipulate XOR and XNOR expressions, compute parity of many inputs and analyse custom defined operators.
topics: Parity as XOR of many inputs
XNOR as equivalence and XNOR chains
Properties of defined and nested operators

nodes.name: Canonical forms
nodes.desc: Minterms, maxterms and canonical forms. Minterm/maxterm indices; SOP/POS and canonical SOP/POS; Σ ↔ Π conversion; expanding terms over missing variables; counting functions (2^{2ⁿ})
nodes.summary: You will be able to write functions in canonical SOP and POS form, convert between minterm and maxterm lists and count Boolean functions.

nodes.name: Universal gates
nodes.desc: Universal gates and functional completeness. NAND-only and NOR-only realisations; minimum gate counts (XOR = 4 NAND, 5 NOR; two-level NAND–NAND / NOR–NOR)
nodes.summary: You will be able to realise any function with only NAND or NOR gates, find minimum gate counts and decide whether a gate set is functionally complete.
topics: NAND and NOR as universal gates
Testing whether a gate set is complete

nodes.name: Circuit analysis
nodes.desc: Analysing gate circuits and timing. Reading multi-level circuits; f = f₁f₂ + f₃ style minterm reasoning; propagation delay; glitches and pulse generation (X·X̄ with delay)
nodes.summary: You will be able to derive the function of multi-level gate circuits and switch networks and reason about propagation delay and timing.

nodes.name: K-maps
nodes.desc: Karnaugh maps (2–4 variables). Map layout and Gray order; adjacency and wrap-around (corners); grouping rules (powers of 2, largest first); SOP from 1s and POS from 0s; reading a given map
nodes.summary: You will be able to minimise functions of up to four variables with Karnaugh maps, producing minimal SOP and POS expressions.

nodes.name: Prime implicants
nodes.desc: Implicants, prime implicants and don't-cares. Implicant / PI / EPI definitions; listing all PIs; counting PIs; selecting a minimal cover (EPIs first, then the cheapest cover)
nodes.summary: You will be able to identify implicants, prime implicants and essential prime implicants and choose a minimal cover using don't-cares.
topics: Multiple minimal covers and cyclic functions

nodes.name: Quine–McCluskey
nodes.desc: Quine–McCluskey, PI charts and larger maps. The Quine–McCluskey tabular method (grouping by weight, combining, PI chart, row and column dominance, Petrick's method in brief); 5-variable maps
nodes.summary: You will be able to minimise functions with the Quine-McCluskey method and prime-implicant charts and handle five- and six-variable maps.

nodes.name: Two-level design
nodes.desc: From minimal forms to gates: cost, NAND/NOR, hazards. Literal and gate cost; SOP vs POS cost; NAND–NAND and NOR–NOR from minimal forms; minimum NOR count for a given function
nodes.summary: You will be able to cost two-level circuits, implement minimal forms with NAND or NOR gates, share terms across outputs and spot static hazards.

nodes.name: Ripple-carry adders
nodes.desc: Half/full adders, subtractors and ripple-carry adders. Half and full adder (from 2 HAs + OR); half and full subtractor; n-bit ripple adder; delay models (2n + 1 etc.); worst-case carry chain
nodes.summary: You will be able to build half and full adders and subtractors, chain them into ripple-carry adders and compute their worst-case delay.
topics: Gate counts in NAND and NOR

nodes.name: Carry look-ahead
nodes.desc: Carry look-ahead adders. Generate/propagate; C_{i+1} = G_i + P_i C_i expanded; two-level CLA delay; group (block) G/P and multi-level CLA; fan-in limits (O(log n))
nodes.summary: You will be able to derive carry look-ahead logic from generate and propagate signals and compare multi-level and hybrid fast adders.

nodes.name: Adder–subtractor
nodes.desc: The adder–subtractor, flag logic and the BCD adder circuit. XOR-controlled adder/subtractor (K and C₀ control lines); the overflow detector (XOR of the last two carries) and flag logic (C, V, S, Z)
nodes.summary: You will be able to design an adder-subtractor with control lines, generate overflow and status flags and build BCD adder hardware.

nodes.name: Multiplier hardware
nodes.desc: Array, sequential and Booth multiplier hardware. The array multiplier (AND array + adder rows); its critical path and Θ(n) delay; hardware cost
nodes.summary: You will be able to design array, sequential and Booth multiplier hardware and estimate their delay and hardware cost.
topics: Partial products and the array multiplier

nodes.name: Combinational design
nodes.desc: Designing combinational circuits; code converters. The design procedure (spec → truth table → K-map → gates); BCD → mod-n, BCD ≥ 5 detectors; excess-3 ↔ BCD; binary ↔ Gray converters; seven-segment (aside)
nodes.summary: You will be able to design combinational circuits from word specifications, including detectors, voting circuits and code converters.

nodes.name: Multiplexers
nodes.desc: Multiplexers and function realisation. 2ⁿ:1 MUX equation; MUX trees; implementing functions (n or n−1 select variables, the residue on the data lines); cascaded/feedback MUX puzzles
nodes.summary: You will be able to analyse multiplexer circuits, implement any Boolean function with a MUX and build large multiplexers from small ones.
topics: The MUX as a universal element

nodes.name: Decoders & encoders
nodes.desc: Decoders, demultiplexers, encoders and priority encoders. N:2ⁿ decoder as a minterm generator; enable inputs and decoder expansion; DEMUX = decoder with data on enable; encoders; priority encoders with a valid bit
nodes.summary: You will be able to use decoders to build functions and memory address logic, expand decoders, and design encoders and priority encoders.

nodes.name: Comparators & parity
nodes.desc: Magnitude comparators and parity circuits. 1-bit and n-bit comparators (equality via XNOR, greater/less cascades); parity generator and checker
nodes.summary: You will be able to design and cascade magnitude comparators, compare numbers by subtraction and build parity generators and checkers.

nodes.name: ROM, PLA & PAL
nodes.desc: ROM, PLA and PAL as combinational logic. ROM = decoder + OR array; sizing a ROM for a truth table (2ⁿ × m); PLA vs PAL; the multiplier-ROM size questions
nodes.summary: You will be able to implement combinational logic with ROMs, PLAs and PALs and size a ROM for a given truth table.
topics: ROM as a stored truth table
Building bigger ROMs from smaller chips

nodes.name: Faults & testing
nodes.desc: Stuck-at faults and test inputs. The stuck-at-0/1 model; activation and propagation; finding a test vector; counting faults
nodes.summary: You will be able to apply the stuck-at fault model and find test vectors that activate and propagate a fault to an output.

nodes.name: Latches
nodes.desc: Feedback, latches and races. Feedback and stable states; SR latch (NOR and NAND, active-low); the forbidden input and oscillation; gated latches; D latch (MUX with feedback)
nodes.summary: You will be able to explain how feedback stores a bit and analyse SR, NAND, gated and D latches, including forbidden inputs.
topics: The NAND latch with active-low inputs
Gated latches and the D latch

nodes.name: Flip-flops
nodes.desc: Flip-flops: SR, JK, D, T, edge triggering and timing. Level vs edge triggering; master–slave; characteristic tables and equations; excitation tables; conversions between types; asynchronous preset/clear
nodes.summary: You will be able to use SR, JK, D and T flip-flops with their characteristic and excitation tables, convert between types and read timing diagrams.
topics: SR, JK, D and T flip-flops

nodes.name: Sequential analysis
nodes.desc: Analysing synchronous sequential circuits. Synchronous vs asynchronous (and why synchronous); excitation and state equations from a circuit; state tables and diagrams
nodes.summary: You will be able to analyse a synchronous sequential circuit by deriving its state equations, state table and state diagram and tracing it clock by clock.
topics: Tracing a circuit clock by clock
Reading outputs at the right time

nodes.name: Ripple counters
nodes.desc: Counter basics and asynchronous (ripple) counters. Mod-N and the flip-flop count ⌈log₂ N⌉; ripple up/down counters; frequency division (f/2ⁿ); ripple delay and max frequency; mod-N by asynchronous clear
nodes.summary: You will be able to design and analyse ripple up, down and mod-N counters and compute their frequency division and ripple delay.

nodes.name: Synchronous counters
nodes.desc: Synchronous counter design. The design procedure with excitation tables; arbitrary sequences; repeated-value sequences (needs extra state bits); Gray and saturating counters
nodes.summary: You will be able to design synchronous counters for arbitrary sequences using excitation tables and check them for self-starting behaviour.
topics: Repeated values needing extra state bits

nodes.name: Shift registers
nodes.desc: Shift registers, ring and Johnson counters, LFSRs. SISO/SIPO/PISO/PIPO; bidirectional/universal; ring (N states) and Johnson (2N states) counters; counter + decoder = ring; LFSR sequences
nodes.summary: You will be able to analyse shift registers, universal registers, ring and Johnson counters and LFSRs and work out their state sequences.

nodes.name: Mealy & Moore FSMs
nodes.desc: Finite state machines: Mealy and Moore. Mealy vs Moore; state diagrams and tables; sequence detectors (overlapping or not); serial adders and serial 2's complementers
nodes.summary: You will be able to design Mealy and Moore machines from word descriptions, including sequence detectors and serial machines, and turn them into circuits.
topics: From words to a state diagram
Shortest input to a target state
From a state machine to a circuit

nodes.name: State minimisation
nodes.desc: State minimisation. Equivalent states; partition refinement; implication tables; incompletely specified machines (brief)
nodes.summary: You will be able to minimise the states of a finite state machine using partition refinement and implication tables.
